doc.title: Tom Lellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 31, 2007

title: Lyric writing: Count to Two and Taken to Heart
summary: He discusses clichés and double entendre, the origin of Count to Two in Eddie Gomez's remark, writing a verse on a plane, and disliking perfunctory bebop lyrics.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I just wanted to ask you, the song you wrote called I think “It Takes Two?”
It’s off, I can’t remember where I put my CDs now. It’s about it only takes the number two.
“Count to Two” thank you. I’m curious, those little turns of a phrase, where do they come from?

You know I don’t know. Trying not to — I don’t want to use clichés as clichés, but I love to take clichés — I love double entendre. My second album was entitled “Double Entendre.” So that’s how much I love them. So I try to just put a little twist on things and maybe turn it around or juxtapose something, you know, like the tunes I like to juxtapose. So I don’t know, and you know that tune specifically came from a comment that Eddie Gomez made. You know we were playing, he’s such a great player and so technically proficient, and I said well let’s play a samba. And I can’t remember how it got — he said, “Oh anybody can play in two.” It’s like he said, “It’s easy to play in two.” And I thought at that time it wasn’t easy for me to play in two. And so that’s actually the basis of that tune. But lyrically that’s what it is. I like to take things that maybe were clichés and take elements of them and mix them in with double entendres and turn ‘em around.
Yeah. Because I saw like almost two story lines in there, or it developed from one thing to the next.
I wonder if it takes — is that a long process for you?

Well I try, I do tweak some, but usually the lyrics come out — not entire intact — but relatively intact. And then they have long gestation periods before, between writing and recording. So I live with them for a while, and then they’ll modify. On the other hand, I wrote the second verse for “Taken to Heart” with the orchestra on the plane to the

Netherlands. Because I only had one verse on the Concord album that I recorded it on and they wanted to redo it, and I said oh I’ve got to get a second verse, so I wrote it on the plane. So some things happen. I sat for three weeks with “Mountain Flight,” couldn’t write a thing and then one day I wrote them in three hours. So it’s very varied. Very.

Absolutely. I like time constraints. They seem to crystallize things. The pressure’s on, okay, you know, maybe I can turn this rock, this piece of coal into a diamond, in that — it’s Superman. So I don’t know, but yeah. I just try — I aspire to write lyrics that I’m not embarrassed singing. That’s really the bottom line. ‘Cause I hear jazz specifically, you know, those bebop tunes and everything, I really have a problem with the lyrics in some jazz tunes.
Yeah. And they weren’t written with that in mind.
Right. They wanted to get to the solo. Everything is to get to the solo.
